Inequalities for convex functions of random points inside and on the boundary of convex bodiesThanks: This work was supported by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Russian Federation (agreement 075-15-2025-344 dated 29/04/2025 for Saint Petersburg Leonhard Euler International Mathematical Institute at PDMI RAS)Thanks: The work was supported by the Theoretical Physics and Mathematics Advancement Foundation “BASIS”Thanks: Supported in part by the Moebius Contest Foundation for Young Scientists

A. S. Tokmachev Address: St. Petersburg Department of Steklov Institute of Mathematics, St. Petersburg, Russia Email address: chief.tokma4eff@yandex.ru
Abstract.

Let KK be a convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let II and BB be random points uniformly distributed inside KK and on its boundary, respectively. We prove that if d=2d=2 and 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B, or if KK is a circumscribed polytope with the center of the inscribed sphere coinciding with 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B, then II is dominated by BB in the convex order. As a consequence, for any function φ\varphi convex in each argument, the expectation 𝔼​φ​(I1,…,Ik)\mathbb{E}\varphi(I_{1},\dots,I_{k}) does not exceed 𝔼​φ​(B1,…,Bk)\mathbb{E}\varphi(B_{1},\dots,B_{k}). This yields, in particular, an inequality between the moments of random chords 𝔼​|I1−I2|p⩽𝔼​|B1−B2|p\mathbb{E}|I_{1}-I_{2}|^{p}\leqslant\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|^{p} for all p⩾1p\geqslant 1, confirming the Zaporozhets–Tarasov conjecture for the indicated class of bodies, and extends to inequalities for mean volumes of random simplices.

Key words and phrases:
Convex body, convex order, convex function, random point, mean distance, geometric inequality, Ohlin’s lemma, Sylvester’s problem

1. Introduction

Let KK be a convex figure in the plane. By this we mean that KK is a convex compact set with nonempty interior; in the sequel we refer to such sets as convex bodies, so as not to introduce separate terminology for the higher-dimensional case.

It is convenient to fix notation for the random points used throughout the paper. Let II be uniformly distributed inside KK (with respect to the Lebesgue measure), and let BB be uniformly distributed on the boundary ∂K\partial K (with respect to the surface measure). Independent copies of these variables will be denoted by I1,I2,…I_{1},I_{2},\dots and B1,B2,…B_{1},B_{2},\dots, respectively.

In 1864, Sylvester posed the following problem [1]: four points I1,I2,I3,I4I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4} are chosen uniformly and independently inside KK. What is the probability that their convex hull conv⁡(I1,I2,I3,I4)\mathrm{conv}(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4}) is a triangle? Clearly, this probability depends on the shape of KK. In 1918, Blaschke [2] proved that for any planar convex body KK,

3512​π2⩽ℙ⁡(conv⁡(I1,I2,I3,I4)​ is a triangle)⩽13,\frac{35}{12\pi^{2}}\leqslant\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{conv}(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4})\text{ is a triangle})\leqslant\frac{1}{3},

where the lower bound is attained on ellipses and the upper bound on triangles.

This problem admits a reformulation in terms of areas. Let area⁡(⋅)\mathrm{area}\,(\cdot) denote the area. A simple computation shows that

ℙ⁡(conv⁡(I1,I2,I3,I4)​ is a triangle)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{conv}(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3},I_{4})\text{ is a triangle}) =4​ℙ​(I4∈conv⁡(I1,I2,I3))=4​𝔼​area​(conv⁡(I1​I2​I3))area​K.\displaystyle=4\mathbb{P}(I_{4}\in\mathrm{conv}(I_{1},I_{2},I_{3}))=4\frac{\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{area}\,(\mathrm{conv}(I_{1}I_{2}I_{3}))}{\mathrm{area}\,K}.

Set α⁡(K)=𝔼​area​(conv⁡(I1​I2​I3))\alpha(K)=\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{area}\,(\mathrm{conv}(I_{1}I_{2}I_{3})). Blaschke’s inequality then becomes

3548​π2≤α⁡(K)area​K≤112,\displaystyle\frac{35}{48\pi^{2}}\leq\frac{\alpha(K)}{\mathrm{area}\,K}\leq\frac{1}{12},

which gives sharp bounds for the normalized mean area of a random triangle with vertices uniformly distributed inside KK.

In [3], the analogous problem for two points was considered: the length of a random segment with endpoints chosen uniformly and independently inside KK, normalized by the perimeter of KK, was estimated. It was shown that for

Δ⁡(K)=𝔼​|I1−I2|\displaystyle\Delta(K)=\mathbb{E}\,|I_{1}-I_{2}|

the following sharp inequalities hold:

(1) 760<Δ⁡(K)per​K<16.\displaystyle\frac{7}{60}<\frac{\Delta(K)}{\mathrm{per}\,K}<\frac{1}{6}.

This result was also extended to higher dimensions, where Δ\Delta is normalized by the mean width of the body. In dimension 2, by Cauchy’s formula (see, e.g., [4]), the mean width coincides with the perimeter multiplied by 1/π1/\pi.

Although both bounds in (1) are strict, they are optimal: the lower bound is asymptotically attained on a sequence of isosceles triangles whose base is fixed while the height tends to zero, and the upper bound is asymptotically attained on a sequence of rectangles degenerating to a segment (which itself has empty interior and does not belong to the class of convex bodies considered here).

Now consider the analogous functionals with points taken on the boundary of the body:

(2) θ⁡(K)\displaystyle\theta(K) =𝔼​|B1−B2|,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\,|B_{1}-B_{2}|,
(3) ψ⁡(K)\displaystyle\psi(K) =𝔼​area​(conv⁡(B1,B2,B3)).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{area}\,(\mathrm{conv}(B_{1},B_{2},B_{3})).

Zaporozhets and Tarasov conjectured that for every convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

(4) Δ⁡(K)<θ⁡(K).\displaystyle\Delta(K)<\theta(K).

To the best of our knowledge, this conjecture remains open even in dimension d=2d=2.

Gusakova and Zaporozhets proposed the following possible approach. They suggested that for any planar convex body,

(5) 16<θ⁡(K)per​K≤2π2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}<\frac{\theta(K)}{\mathrm{per}\,K}\leq\frac{2}{\pi^{2}},

where equality in the upper bound holds if and only if KK is a disk, while the lower bound is unattainable in the class of convex bodies but is reached on a segment, which can be approximated by rectangles. Clearly, the lower bound in (5) together with the upper bound in (1) would immediately imply (4).

In the author’s works [5, 6], the upper bounds in conjecture (5) and related results for ψ\psi were proved. Namely, the disk maximizes both the normalized mean distance between two boundary points and the normalized mean area of a triangle with three boundary vertices, for a fixed perimeter.

In 2025, A. S. Lotnikov [7] obtained a number of results related to conjecture (4) for centrally symmetric planar bodies. He showed that for such bodies not only does Δ⁡(K)<θ⁡(K)\Delta(K)<\theta(K) hold, but a stronger stochastic domination statement is true: for any n>1n>1, 𝔼​|B1​B2|n⩾𝔼​|I1​I2|n\mathbb{E}|B_{1}B_{2}|^{n}\geqslant\mathbb{E}|I_{1}I_{2}|^{n}. He also established exact formulas relating moments of interior and boundary chords for circumscribed polygons.

The aim of the present paper is to extend the chord-length inequality to a wider class of bodies. We show that in the plane, the inequality 𝔼​|I1​I2|p⩽𝔼​|B1​B2|p\mathbb{E}|I_{1}I_{2}|^{p}\leqslant\mathbb{E}|B_{1}B_{2}|^{p} for all p⩾1p\geqslant 1 holds under the single condition 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B (which is automatically true for centrally symmetric bodies). Moreover, we prove a substantially more general fact: the inequality holds for arbitrary functions convex in each argument. As a corollary, we obtain an analogous inequality for the mean volume of a random simplex with vertices chosen inside and on the boundary of the body.

2. Main results

Our main result is the following theorem.

Theorem 1.

Let KK be a convex body in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying one of the following:

  • •

    d=2d=2 and 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B;

  • •

    KK is a circumscribed polytope whose inscribed sphere center OO coincides with 𝔼​I\mathbb{E}I and 𝔼​B\mathbb{E}B.

Let φ:(ℝd)k→ℝ\varphi:(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{k}\to\mathbb{R} be a function convex in each argument. Then

(6) 𝔼​φ​(I1,…,Ik)⩽𝔼​φ​(B1,…,Bk),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\varphi(I_{1},\ldots,I_{k})\leqslant\mathbb{E}\varphi(B_{1},\ldots,B_{k}),

where I1,…,IkI_{1},\dots,I_{k} and B1,…,BkB_{1},\dots,B_{k} are independent samples uniformly distributed inside KK and on ∂K\partial K, respectively.

Taking φ⁡(x,y)=|x−y|p\varphi(x,y)=|x-y|^{p} (p⩾1p\geqslant 1) gives a generalization of Lotnikov’s result.

Corollary 1.

Under the conditions of Theorem 1, for any p⩾1p\geqslant 1,

(7) 𝔼​|I1−I2|p⩽𝔼​|B1−B2|p.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}|I_{1}-I_{2}|^{p}\leqslant\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|^{p}.

For p=1p=1, Corollary 1 confirms the Zaporozhets–Tarasov conjecture for the bodies in question.

Another example of a function convex in each argument is

φ⁡(x1,…,xn)=(vold​(conv⁡{x1,…,xn}))p,p⩾1.\varphi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=(\mathrm{vol}\,_{d}(\mathrm{conv}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}))^{p},\qquad p\geqslant 1.
Corollary 2.

Under the conditions of Theorem 1, for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and p⩾1p\geqslant 1,

(8) 𝔼⁡[vold​(conv⁡{I1,…,In})p]⩽𝔼⁡[vold​(conv⁡{B1,…,Bn})p].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{vol}\,_{d}(\mathrm{conv}\{I_{1},\ldots,I_{n}\})^{p}\bigr]\leqslant\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{vol}\,_{d}(\mathrm{conv}\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{n}\})^{p}\bigr].

For n=d+1n=d+1 and p=1p=1, this yields α⁡(K)⩽ψ⁡(K)\alpha(K)\leqslant\psi(K) for the mean volumes of random simplices with vertices inside and on the boundary.

3. Reduction to the convex order

The key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1 is the convex order between the distributions of II and BB. Recall that X⪯c​xYX\preceq_{cx}Y (in the convex order) if 𝔼​φ​(X)⩽𝔼​φ​(Y)\mathbb{E}\varphi(X)\leqslant\mathbb{E}\varphi(Y) for every convex function φ\varphi. By Strassen’s theorem [8], X⪯c​xYX\preceq_{cx}Y is equivalent to the existence of a coupling with 𝔼⁡[Y∣X]=X\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X almost surely; in particular, 𝔼​X=𝔼​Y\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}Y is necessary.

To prove Theorem 1 it suffices to establish I⪯c​xBI\preceq_{cx}B; the full statement then follows from independence and properties of conditional expectations. Thus we need only prove:

Theorem 2 (Convex order for II and BB).

Under the same assumptions on KK as in Theorem 1,

(9) I⪯c​xB,\displaystyle I\preceq_{cx}B,

i.e., 𝔼​φ​(I)⩽𝔼​φ​(B)\mathbb{E}\varphi(I)\leqslant\mathbb{E}\varphi(B) for every convex φ:ℝd→ℝ\varphi\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}.

The case of a circumscribed polytope is due to Pasteczka [10] (Theorem 2). The next section contains the proof for d=2d=2, which is the main contribution of this note.

4. Proof of Theorem 2 for d=2d=2

We need two auxiliary facts: the Ohlin lemma and a characterization of the convex order via one-dimensional projections.

Lemma 1 (Ohlin [11]).

Let XX and YY be integrable random variables with 𝔼​X=𝔼​Y\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}Y. If their distribution functions FXF_{X} and FYF_{Y} cross exactly once, with FX⩽FYF_{X}\leqslant F_{Y} to the left of the crossing point and FX⩾FYF_{X}\geqslant F_{Y} to the right, then 𝔼​f​(X)⩽𝔼​f​(Y)\mathbb{E}f(X)\leqslant\mathbb{E}f(Y) for every convex f:ℝ→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}.

The next fact is well known (see, e.g., [9]).

Lemma 2.

For X,Y∈ℝdX,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, one has X⪯c​xYX\preceq_{cx}Y if and only if for every unit vector u∈Sd−1u\in S^{d-1} and every convex f:ℝ→ℝf\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R},

(10) 𝔼​f​(⟨X,u⟩)⩽𝔼​f​(⟨Y,u⟩),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f(\langle X,u\rangle)\leqslant\mathbb{E}f(\langle Y,u\rangle),

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is the scalar product.

Now we prove the theorem. Let d=2d=2 and 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B. Fix a unit vector u∈S1u\in S^{1} and let Iu=⟨I,u⟩I_{u}=\langle I,u\rangle, Bu=⟨B,u⟩B_{u}=\langle B,u\rangle be the projections onto the line spanned by uu. We verify the Ohlin condition for IuI_{u} and BuB_{u}.

First, 𝔼​I=𝔼​B\mathbb{E}I=\mathbb{E}B implies

𝔼​Iu=⟨𝔼​I,u⟩=⟨𝔼​B,u⟩=𝔼​Bu.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}I_{u}=\langle\mathbb{E}I,u\rangle=\langle\mathbb{E}B,u\rangle=\mathbb{E}B_{u}.

Second, by Lemma 2 of [12], the distribution functions FIuF_{I_{u}} and FBuF_{B_{u}} cross exactly once, with the sign pattern required in Ohlin’s lemma (the crossing point x0x_{0} is the projection of the “widest part” of KK onto this line). Hence,

𝔼​f​(Iu)⩽𝔼​f​(Bu)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f(I_{u})\leqslant\mathbb{E}f(B_{u})

for every convex ff. By Lemma 2, this yields I⪯c​xBI\preceq_{cx}B, completing the proof of the two-dimensional case.
